clue.text: Old Rachel hid sort of Byronic hero (66)

indicators.note: 'sort of' suggests a loose version of the letters of Old Rachel hid, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: An old woman called Rachel concealed a man of the Byronic heroic type.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sort of' rearranges OLDRACHELHID. Byron's poem Childe Harold's Pilgrimage gives its wandering title figure as the original Byronic hero; the (66) is part of the printed clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Byron's long poem follows this melancholy wandering youth, the model for the brooding protagonist named after the poet.

clue.text: "You will worship my spear as a god" bragged this transsexual Greek

definitions.text: "You will worship my spear as a god" bragged this transsexual Greek

parts.words: "You will worship my spear as a god" bragged this transsexual Greek
parts.note: a Lapith of Greek myth, born the girl Caenis and changed by Poseidon into an invulnerable man, who set up a spear and ordered people to worship it

explanation.surface: A boastful Greek who changed sex demands that a spear be worshipped.
explanation.definitionFit: Myth tells of the Lapith warrior, once a woman, who arrogantly demanded divine honours for his weapon.

clue.text: List of Firbank's proclivities

definitions.meaning: a ship that lists leans to one side
a proclivity is a leaning; Ronald Firbank wrote the novel Inclinations

explanation.surface: An inventory of the tastes of the novelist Ronald Firbank.
explanation.definitionFit: A ship's lean and a person's tendency are both senses of a slope or leaning.

clue.text: King's son featured in garbled ad lib (Anon)

indicators.note: garbled speech is jumbled, so the letters of ad lib and Anon are mixed up

explanation.surface: A prince appears in a muddled improvisation by an anonymous writer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'garbled' rearranges ADLIBANON. In Macbeth he is the younger son of King Duncan.
explanation.definitionFit: In Shakespeare's Macbeth he is the younger son of the murdered Scottish monarch Duncan.

clue.text: Heads put together for some really earthy drama

indicators.note: 'some' asks for only part of the phrase really earthy drama, its letters running across the words

explanation.surface: Writers collaborate on a properly down-to-earth play.
explanation.walkthrough: 'some' points to a run spanning earthy and drama.
explanation.definitionFit: The monster of Greek myth grew many heads on one body, a cluster of them joined together.

clue.text: Hurrying about, say, like Grishkin's eye

indicators.note: 'say' means the word for hurrying about is spoken, giving the sound of the answer

parts.note: rushing about, clipped in speech to rushin'

explanation.surface: Someone dashing around, perhaps, resembles the eye of a woman in a poem.
explanation.walkthrough: In T. S. Eliot's Whispers of Immortality, Grishkin's eye is described by its nationality: 'her Russian eye is underlined for emphasis'.
explanation.definitionFit: Eliot's poem gives the seductive Grishkin an eye from the country of Moscow, so the adjective of nationality fits.

clue.text: One line could suggest a sort of Latin verse

indicators.note: the letters of one line could suggest another word when rearranged

explanation.surface: A single line of poetry hints at a kind of classical metre.
explanation.definitionFit: Medieval Latin hexameters with internal rhyme between the middle and end of each line carry this name.

clue.text: Rattigan's notorious controversy

definitions.meaning: Terence Rattigan's last play, about a real 1930s murder trial
a famous case that arouses public debate

explanation.surface: The playwright Terence Rattigan's infamous dispute.
explanation.definitionFit: The French phrase for a famous case is used in English for any scandal that stirs wide public argument, and Rattigan took it as a title.

clue.text: Possibly non-lace city of the Normans

indicators.note: 'Possibly' says the letters of non-lace may be put in another order

explanation.surface: A Norman town that, oddly, is not famous for lacework.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Possibly' rearranges NONLACE. The joke is that this town in Normandy is famous for its needlepoint lace.
explanation.definitionFit: This town lies in Normandy, in north-west France, a historic Norman centre.

clue.text: Rulers of the French places for whom benevolence was a byword

parts.note: de is French for of
spots are places or locations

explanation.surface: Kings of France were known for their benevolence.
explanation.walkthrough: The rest of the clue points to 'benevolent' as their usual epithet, the enlightened absolutists of eighteenth-century Europe.
explanation.definitionFit: Absolute monarchs and tyrants are sovereigns who govern alone.

clue.text: Chapman's theatrical agents described as dim

parts.note: dim means slow-witted, simple
secret agents are spies, spymen

explanation.surface: Actors' agents in a play are portrayed as unintelligent.
explanation.walkthrough: John Chapman's Whitehall farce of 1958 is titled with these two words.
explanation.definitionFit: The title of John Chapman's Brian Rix farce is this phrase, a stage comedy about bumbling secret agents.

clue.text: Iris Murdoch wrote it to accompany something

definitions.text: Iris Murdoch wrote it to accompany something

parts.words: Iris Murdoch wrote it to accompany something
parts.note: Iris Murdoch's 1957 short story's title is something followed by the missing word

explanation.surface: A novelist composed a piece as accompaniment.
explanation.definitionFit: Murdoch's story Something ___ needs this adjective after its first word to complete the title.

clue.text: I'm held by a faddish theory Stahl's

indicators.note: 'held by' means the words I'm sit inside the other pieces

parts.note: an is the form of the indefinite article before a vowel
an ism is a faddish doctrine or creed
taken as written without the apostrophe

explanation.surface: A trendy scientific idea grips me.
explanation.walkthrough: Georg Stahl, the German chemist, held that the soul animates the body.
explanation.definitionFit: Stahl taught that a vital soul is the source of life in the body, a doctrine known by this name.

clue.text: Dramatis personae have a point in hereditary class

parts.note: the dramatis personae are the characters, the cast of a play
E is east, a point of the compass

explanation.surface: The characters of a play make a point about social rank.
explanation.definitionFit: In Hindu society a person's rigid social group is fixed by birth; T. W. Robertson's play of that title is also nodded at.

clue.text: Composer to include offer for cash

parts.note: to add in is to include
to sell is to offer for money

explanation.surface: A musician agrees to put an item up for sale.
explanation.walkthrough: Richard Addinsell wrote the Warsaw Concerto.
explanation.definitionFit: Richard Addinsell was an English writer of film music, best known for the Warsaw Concerto.

clue.text: He thought, therefore he was

parts.note: plays on the French philosopher's maxim 'I think, therefore I am', put into the past tense

explanation.surface: A man's thinking proved his existence.
explanation.definitionFit: The seventeenth-century philosopher's cogito ergo sum is recast here in the third person and past tense.

clue.text: Bardell and Pickwick might be construed as tilting

indicators.note: construing a phrase interprets it differently, so the letters of as tilting are rearranged

explanation.surface: Two Dickens characters could be seen as jousting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'might be construed' rearranges ASTILTING. Bardell v Pickwick is the breach-of-promise suit in Dickens's Pickwick Papers.
explanation.definitionFit: Mrs Bardell sued Mr Pickwick in a famous court case, making the pair parties to a lawsuit.

clue.text: Its participants may feel they have been framed

definitions.text: Its participants may feel they have been framed

parts.words: Its participants may feel they have been framed
parts.note: framed suggests wrongly accused, but the people in a posed stage picture are held motionless as if within a picture frame

explanation.surface: People involved feel they have been set up by false evidence.
explanation.definitionFit: A living picture has performers standing still and silent as though in a painting.

clue.text: French puppet said to be from lions, though hardly

definitions.text: French puppet said to be from lions, though hardly

parts.words: French puppet said to be from lions, though hardly
parts.note: lions sounds like Lyons, the city where this puppet originated; 'hardly' admits the puppet is no lion

explanation.surface: A French marionette is supposedly descended from big cats, which is unlikely.
explanation.definitionFit: The Lyon glove-puppet created by Laurent Mourguet gave its name to French puppet theatre.

clue.text: A party-goer of Eliot's? or a character from Scenes from Clerical Life?

definitions.meaning: a figure at a party in a work by T. S. Eliot

definitions.text: a character from Scenes from Clerical Life?
definitions.meaning: a figure in George Eliot's first book of fiction

explanation.surface: Is this guest at an Eliot gathering also a figure in an early Victorian novel?
explanation.walkthrough: The two Eliots are different writers: T. S. and George.
explanation.definitionFit: The surname belongs to a figure in each Eliot's work, one modern poet-dramatist, one Victorian novelist.

clue.text: Dramatic performance by Dane likely to rock audiences?

definitions.text: Dramatic performance by Dane likely to rock audiences?

parts.words: Dramatic performance by Dane likely to rock audiences?
parts.note: Clemence Dane wrote a 1926 play named after a hard stone, so it is literally a rock

explanation.surface: A Danish actor's show will stun theatregoers.
explanation.walkthrough: Dane is not a Dane but the playwright Clemence Dane.
explanation.definitionFit: Clemence Dane's play bears the name of a hard igneous stone, hence likely to rock.

clue.text: Tolkien recorded the travels of this voyager saint"

definitions.text: Tolkien recorded the travels of this voyager saint"

parts.words: Tolkien recorded the travels of this voyager saint"
parts.note: Tolkien's poem Imram retells the sea voyage of the Irish navigator monk

explanation.surface: Tolkien wrote about a holy man's sea journey.
explanation.definitionFit: The sixth-century Irish monk 'the Navigator' is said to have sailed the Atlantic, and Tolkien's poem Imram tells his voyage.

clue.text: George Folansbee, booster of Zip City

definitions.text: George Folansbee, booster of Zip City

parts.words: George Folansbee, booster of Zip City
parts.note: Sinclair Lewis's realtor George F., boastful promoter of the city of Zenith, nicknamed Zip City

explanation.surface: A man named George promotes his home town.
explanation.definitionFit: Sinclair Lewis's 1922 novel is titled with the surname of this smug, boosterish Midwestern businessman.

clue.text: With which the Spanish modify the first of November

definitions.text: With which the Spanish modify the first of November

parts.words: With which the Spanish modify the first of November
parts.note: the first of November is the letter N, which Spanish writes with a wavy mark above it to make a separate letter

explanation.surface: Spaniards change an early date in the eleventh month.
explanation.definitionFit: The wavy diacritic placed over n in Spanish turns it into a palatal ñ.

clue.text: Where to pose Barbara Pym's question?

definitions.text: Where to pose Barbara Pym's question?

parts.words: Where to pose Barbara Pym's question?
parts.note: Barbara Pym's novel is An Academic Question, which would be asked in a place of learning

explanation.surface: Asks where to put a novelist's query.
explanation.definitionFit: A school or learned society is where an academic question belongs.

clue.text: Manning's priesthood

parts.note: Cardinal Manning wrote The ___ Priesthood, the missing word meaning everlasting

explanation.surface: A priest's role as described by Cardinal Manning.
explanation.definitionFit: Cardinal Manning's book on holy orders is The Eternal Priesthood, the adjective meaning everlasting.

clue.text: Governess in Walpole's stronghold

parts.note: Hugh Walpole's novel The Fortress, the stronghold, has a governess of this name

explanation.surface: A children's tutor lives in a castle.
explanation.definitionFit: Stronghold stands for The Fortress, Hugh Walpole's Herries novel, in which she is the governess.

clue.text: Prince's minder led insurgent astray

indicators.note: going astray means wandering off course, so the letters of led insurgent are scattered

explanation.surface: A rebel's leader took the wrong path.
explanation.walkthrough: 'astray' rearranges LEDINSURGENT. With Rosencrantz he is sent to watch over Prince Hamlet.
explanation.definitionFit: In Hamlet, the king sets two of the prince's old schoolfellows to keep watch on him, and he is one.
